NBC: Latvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition

SearchSearchFacebookTwitterEmailSMSBlue SkyWhatsappPrintRedditFlipboardPinterestLinkedinLatest StoriesMeet the PressU.S. NewsWorldSportsBusinessHealthShoppingTiplineEuropeLatvian PM on track to lead pro-Ukraine coalition after election winThe leader’s pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia ​should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on tackling cost-of-living issues.Listen to this article with a free profile00:0000:00Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs waits for the first exit poll results Saturday.Wojtek Radawanski / AFP via Getty ImagesShareAdd NBC News to GoogleOct. 4, 2026, 3:57 AM EDT / Source: ReutersBy ReutersRIGA, Latvia — Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs was set to retain power and form a pro-Ukrainian coalition after his centrist United List secured the biggest parliamentary election victory since Latvia regained independence in 1991.

With 97% of ballots counted ⁠after Saturday’s election in the NATO and European Union country bordering Russia, United List was on 35.3%, enough for 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament.

A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray Ukrainian military drones flew undetected into Latvia.

Latvia’s economy has ⁠underperformed its Baltic neighbors for more than a decade, and ​Kulbergs ⁠has vowed to improve governance, cut red tape and reduce public spending, political scientist Roberts Kits said.

“Kulbergs played on being a get-things-done type of guy and has persuaded the voters that ⁠he can do things differently, bring some fresh energy,” he said.

“This means the responsibility is huge. ​People expect ⁠him to deliver, but the question remains ‌whether he has the team to do it.”

United List appeared able to secure a parliamentary majority with either the nationalist National Alliance or the liberal Progressives, Kits said.

Kulbergs ‌pledged continuing support to Ukraine and to keep a hard line ‌toward Moscow.

Yes, it can bring some extra money, but it’s a weakness Russia might exploit,” he told reporters at his party’s headquarters on election night as supporters celebrated the scale of the win.

“It’s remarkably good. ⁠I was not expecting such a result,” Kulbergs said.

United List was followed by the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First, which was on 13.1%. Latvia First had courted the country’s substantial ethnic Russian minority in the run-up to the vote.

Third in the ranking was the pro-Russian Sovereign Power party, on 11.7%, followed by the National Alliance, which promotes a hard-line approach to the Kremlin, at 8.9%.

Throughout his campaign, Kulbergs promised more anti-drone capability for Latvia and to maintain defense spending at 5% ‌of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO.

His pro-Kremlin rivals said Latvia ​should stop any aid to Ukraine and instead focus on tackling cost-of-living issues, particularly among the ‌country’s Russian-speaking minority.

Although pro-Russian parties increased their ⁠representation, Kits said they remained sidelined and were unlikely to influence government policy.

Latvia’s ethnic Russian minority ⁠is split between those who oppose Moscow’s war in Ukraine and others who voice frustration with policies at home aimed at limiting ‌their influence on public life, which ​many of them see as discriminatory.

Latvia, with a population ‌of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea ​and Russia and Belarus to the east, with E.U. and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south.
